code.title: Managed memory is freed for you; a borrowed handle is not

followUps:
Treat it as an unmanaged resource. The SqlConnection object itself is ordinary managed memory, but it holds a network socket and a session on the database server, and the garbage collector knows nothing about those.

Example: a connection pool has 100 connections by default. If each request opens one and forgets to dispose it, request 101 waits for a free connection and fails with a timeout, even though memory use looks normal. So always write await using var conn = ...; disposing returns the connection to the pool at once.

The file handle stays open until the garbage collector happens to finalize the stream, and nobody knows when that will be.

  • Until then the file stays locked. A second attempt to open it for writing fails with an IOException saying the file is used by another process.
  • If a StreamWriter sits on top, the last buffered text may never reach the disk.
  • Under load, thousands of open handles can hit the operating system limit.

The memory of the object is small, so the problem does not show as high memory. Fix: using var fs = File.OpenRead(path);

No. The GC never calls Dispose; it only frees memory.

What the GC can do is run a finalizer, if the class has one. Well-written wrappers such as SafeFileHandle have a finalizer that releases the native handle as a last safety net. But it runs late (seconds or hours later, only after a collection), on a separate finalizer thread, and not at all for your own classes that have no finalizer.

So the rule is: if a type implements IDisposable and you created it, you dispose it, normally with using.

code.title: using calls Dispose even when the code throws

followUps:
The container disposes it. Whoever creates a disposable object owns it, and here the creator is the container.

  • Scoped services are disposed when the scope ends, which in ASP.NET Core is the end of the request.
  • Singletons are disposed when the application shuts down.
  • Transient disposables are tracked by the scope they were resolved from and disposed with it.

So never call Dispose on an injected service: the next user of the same instance would get a dead object. One exception: an instance you built yourself and registered with AddSingleton(instance) is yours to dispose.

Dispose cleans up synchronously, and DisposeAsync does the same job but can wait for I/O without blocking a thread.

Cleanup sometimes needs I/O: a stream must flush its last bytes to disk, a database connection must send a closing message. With Dispose a thread is blocked during that. DisposeAsync (from IAsyncDisposable) returns a ValueTask and is called by await using:

await using var stream = File.Create(path);
await stream.WriteAsync(data, ct);
// DisposeAsync flushes here, no thread blocked

If a type offers both, use await using in async code.

Because each new HttpClient brings its own connection pool, so disposing it throws away connections that could have been reused.

A closed socket is not free at once: the operating system keeps the port reserved for a while (up to a few minutes). At 200 requests per second with one client per request, the machine runs out of ports and calls fail with socket errors, although the code looks correct.

Fix: register clients with AddHttpClient (IHttpClientFactory), which reuses handlers and recycles them so DNS changes are noticed. Or keep one long-lived client with PooledConnectionLifetime set to a few minutes.

code.title: The waiter: waiting one by one vs handing in all orders first

followUps:
No. await never creates a thread; it only says "continue this method when that task is finished".

If the task is already finished, the method simply carries on. If not, the method saves its place and returns, and the current thread is free for other work. For real I/O (a database call, an HTTP call) there is no thread at all during the wait: the operating system signals when the answer arrives, and any free pool thread runs the rest.

Example: 1,000 requests each waiting 2 seconds on SQL need about 1,000 blocked threads with synchronous code, and only a handful with await.

It returns Task, which means "I will finish later, and I will tell you if I failed".

Return typeUse
TaskNo result. The caller can await it and catch its exception
Task<T>A result of type T
ValueTask / ValueTask<T>Hot paths that often finish synchronously
async voidOnly event handlers such as a button click

Never use async void elsewhere: the caller cannot await it, and an exception inside it can crash the process.

A good answer is short and has numbers. Here is the shape to copy.

"Our order API called a payment service that took about 800 ms. The code used a synchronous HTTP call, so each request held a thread for 800 ms. At around 250 requests at the same time the thread pool ran out, requests queued, and response times went from 1 second to 15 seconds while CPU stayed under 20%. We made the path async from the controller down to the HTTP call. The same load then ran on about 20 threads and the 95th percentile came back to 1.1 seconds."

Say what was slow, what you changed, and the before and after numbers. Note that one request did not get faster; the server handled more of them.

code.title: Waiting work (WhenAll) vs computing work (Parallel.For)

followUps:
Yes. Concurrency only needs several tasks to be in progress in the same period; it does not need them to run at the same instant.

On one core the operating system gives each thread a short time slice (a few milliseconds) and switches between them, so 3 downloads and a typing user all make progress. Async code does the same with even less: one thread starts 3 HTTP calls, and handles each answer as it arrives. JavaScript in a browser works this way on a single thread.

What one core cannot give you is parallelism: a calculation that needs 4 seconds of CPU still takes 4 seconds, however you split it.

It is asynchrony and concurrency, not parallelism.

The 3 calls are in progress during the same period (concurrent), and no thread is blocked while waiting for them (asynchronous). But your CPU is not computing 3 things at once: the work is happening on 3 other servers and your process only waits.

Numbers: calls of 200, 300 and 250 ms take 750 ms one after another and about 300 ms with Task.WhenAll, the time of the slowest call. This works the same on a 1-core machine, which shows it is not parallelism.

Because the database call is waiting work, and Task.Run is a tool for computing work: it only moves the wait to another pool thread.

  • With a synchronous query inside Task.Run, a pool thread is still blocked for the whole query. You freed one thread and blocked another, plus the cost of the hand-over.
  • With an async query inside Task.Run, you add an extra thread hop for no gain. Just await the query directly.

In ASP.NET Core the request already runs on a pool thread, so there is nothing to free. The one valid use is a desktop app with a library that has only synchronous calls: Task.Run keeps the UI thread responsive.

code.title: A hand-written state machine: what the compiler builds for await

followUps:
ConfigureAwait(false) tells the await "do not bring me back to the original context; continue on any pool thread".

It matters where a SynchronizationContext exists: WPF, WinForms, MAUI and the old ASP.NET. There, a normal await returns to the UI or request thread. If that thread is blocked on .Result, you get a deadlock; ConfigureAwait(false) avoids it and saves the hop.

ASP.NET Core has no such context, so in application code it changes nothing and you can leave it out. Keep it in library code, because you do not know which kind of app will call the library.

Yes. Everything before the first await that actually has to wait runs synchronously on the caller's thread, like a normal method.

async Task LoadAsync()
{
    Thread.Sleep(3000);     // blocks the caller for 3 s
    await Task.Delay(10);   // first real pause is here
}

Two results follow. First, heavy work at the top of an async method blocks the caller, for example it freezes a UI. Second, the caller gets the Task back only when the method reaches that first pause. An exception thrown before it is still stored in the task, so the caller sees it at its own await, not at the call.

They live in the state machine object, as fields, and that object is on the heap while the method is paused.

The compiler turns each local that is needed after an await into a field of the generated state machine. The machine starts as a struct on the stack. At the first await that really waits, it is copied to the heap, because the stack frame disappears when the method returns to its caller.

Practical effect: a 10 MB byte[] local that is still used after an await cannot be collected during the wait. And a method that finishes without waiting allocates nothing for the machine.

code.title: Thread, thread pool, Task and ValueTask side by side

followUps:
No. A Task is a promise of a result, and many tasks have no thread at all while they are in progress.

  • Task.Run(() => Compute()): yes, a pool thread runs the code.
  • httpClient.GetAsync(url), Task.Delay(1000), an async SQL query: no thread while waiting. The operating system or a timer completes the task later.
  • A task from TaskCompletionSource: completed by whoever calls SetResult.

Example: 10,000 Task.Delay(5000) tasks run happily in a process with 10 threads. 10,000 Thread.Sleep(5000) calls would need 10,000 threads and about 10 GB of stack space.

The behaviour is undefined: you may get the right value, a wrong value, or an InvalidOperationException.

A ValueTask can be backed by a reusable object (an IValueTaskSource) that the library takes back and uses for the next operation as soon as you have read the result. A second await then reads state that belongs to someone else.

Rules for a ValueTask:

  • await it exactly once;
  • do not call .Result before it is complete;
  • do not await it from two places at the same time.

If you need any of those, call .AsTask() once and use the Task.

Rarely: when the work needs a worker of its own for a long time, or needs thread settings that a pool thread must not have.

  • A loop that runs for the life of the process, such as reading a serial port or a blocking message consumer. Parking it on a pool thread takes a worker away from everyone else.
  • You need a different priority, a larger stack, or a foreground thread that keeps the process alive.
  • Old COM components that require an STA thread.

Even then, Task.Factory.StartNew(Loop, TaskCreationOptions.LongRunning) often does the job: it creates a dedicated thread and still gives you a task to observe. If the loop is async, use a BackgroundService.

code.title: Two async mistakes: awaiting one by one, and forgetting to await

followUps:
Because WPF has a SynchronizationContext that sends the rest of an async method back to the one UI thread, and ASP.NET Core has no such context.

  1. The button handler calls LoadAsync().Result. The UI thread blocks.
  2. Inside LoadAsync, the await finishes and wants to continue on the UI thread.
  3. The UI thread is waiting for LoadAsync. Each waits for the other, forever.

In ASP.NET Core the continuation runs on any free pool thread, so step 2 succeeds and there is no deadlock. It is still wrong: the request holds a blocked thread for the whole call, and under load that leads to thread-pool starvation.

No. A DbContext is not thread-safe and allows only one operation at a time.

EF Core detects it and throws InvalidOperationException: "A second operation was started on this context instance before a previous operation completed". Without that check, the change tracker and the single database connection would be corrupted.

Two correct options:

  • Await the queries one after the other on the same context. Simple and usually fast enough.
  • If they really must overlap, give each query its own context from IDbContextFactory<T>:
await using var db1 = await factory.CreateDbContextAsync(ct);
await using var db2 = await factory.CreateDbContextAsync(ct);
await Task.WhenAll(db1.Orders.CountAsync(ct), db2.Users.CountAsync(ct));

Hand the work to a background worker through a queue; do not start an un-awaited task from the request.

A fire-and-forget Task.Run has three problems: the request's scoped services (such as the DbContext) are disposed while it still runs, its exceptions are lost, and a deployment kills it half-way.

  1. The endpoint writes a small job to a bounded Channel<T> and returns 202 Accepted.
  2. A BackgroundService reads the channel, creates its own scope with IServiceScopeFactory, does the work and logs failures.
  3. If the job must survive a restart (an email, a payment), use a durable queue such as Azure Service Bus, or the outbox pattern.

code.title: Retry with growing delays, and a timeout through a CancellationToken

followUps:
Because it can hold a timer and callback registrations, and those stay alive until you dispose it.

  • CancelAfter(30 s) or new CancellationTokenSource(timeout) creates a timer.
  • CreateLinkedTokenSource(parent) registers a callback on the parent token. If the parent lives a long time (the application-stopping token, for example), every undisposed linked source stays referenced by it. One per request means memory grows steadily.
using var cts = CancellationTokenSource
    .CreateLinkedTokenSource(ct);
cts.CancelAfter(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30));

The using removes the registration and the timer when the method ends.

A circuit breaker stops calling a service that keeps failing, for a short period, and fails at once instead. A retry does the opposite: it calls again.

RetryCircuit breaker
Helps withA short blipA service that is down or overloaded
Effect on the other sideMore callsFewer calls, time to recover

Example: after 5 failures in 30 seconds the breaker opens for 30 seconds and every call fails in 1 ms. Then it lets one trial call through (half-open); success closes it. In .NET use Microsoft.Extensions.Http.Resilience (built on Polly), and put the retry outside the breaker.

Only if the operation is idempotent, meaning that sending it twice has the same effect as sending it once. A plain "create order" POST is not.

The danger: the server creates the order, the answer is lost on the network, the client times out and retries, and the customer now has 2 orders and 2 charges.

Make it safe with an idempotency key:

  1. The client creates a GUID once and sends it in an Idempotency-Key header on every attempt.
  2. The server stores the key with the result, under a unique index.
  3. A repeat with the same key returns the stored result and creates nothing.

GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent by design, so they can be retried.

code.title: WhenAll with two failures, and WhenAny as a timeout

followUps:
Nothing happens to it: it keeps running to the end, using its connection and memory, and its result or exception is simply ignored.

WhenAny only tells you who finished first. It does not cancel anyone. So after a timeout built with WhenAny, the slow query still runs on the database for another 30 seconds.

To really stop the loser, give both tasks a token and cancel it:

using var cts = CancellationTokenSource.CreateLinkedTokenSource(ct);
Task<Order> work = LoadAsync(cts.Token);
if (await Task.WhenAny(work, Task.Delay(2000, cts.Token)) != work)
{
    cts.Cancel();              // stop the slow call
    throw new TimeoutException();
}

Simpler still: await work.WaitAsync(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(2), ct) or cts.CancelAfter.

Use Parallel.ForEachAsync with MaxDegreeOfParallelism = 10, or put a SemaphoreSlim(10) around each call.

WhenAll has no limit of its own: 5,000 ids means 5,000 calls at once, which empties the connection pool or gets you rate-limited.

var gate = new SemaphoreSlim(10);
var tasks = ids.Select(async id =>
{
    await gate.WaitAsync(ct);
    try { return await LoadAsync(id, ct); }
    finally { gate.Release(); }
});
var results = await Task.WhenAll(tasks);

With 5,000 calls of 100 ms each this takes about 5,000 / 10 × 0.1 = 50 seconds and never has more than 10 calls in flight. Use the semaphore version when you need the results back in order.

.Wait() throws an AggregateException that wraps the real error, while await throws the real error itself.

CallWhat you catchBlocks a thread?
await taskThe original exception, e.g. HttpRequestExceptionNo
task.Wait(), task.ResultAggregateException; the real one is in InnerExceptionsYes
task.GetAwaiter().GetResult()The original exceptionYes

So a catch (HttpRequestException) that works with await is silently skipped with .Wait(). That is one more reason not to block on tasks.

code.title: A shared counter: unsafe, Interlocked, lock, ConcurrentDictionary

followUps:
Because count++ is three separate steps, and another thread can run between them.

  1. Read count into a register.
  2. Add 1 to the register.
  3. Write the register back to count.

Example with count = 5: thread A reads 5, thread B reads 5, A writes 6, B writes 6. Two increments happened and the value went up by 1. With 4 threads doing 200,000 increments each you can easily end near 500,000 when you expected 800,000.

Fix: Interlocked.Increment(ref count) does all three steps as one CPU instruction, or put the line inside a lock. Marking the field volatile does not fix it.

Because a lock belongs to the thread that took it, and after an await the method may continue on a different thread, which cannot release a lock it does not own.

The compiler stops you with an error. There is a second danger too: holding a lock across a slow wait makes every other caller queue behind it.

Use SemaphoreSlim, which has no owner thread and can be awaited:

private readonly SemaphoreSlim _gate = new(1, 1);

await _gate.WaitAsync(ct);
try { await RefreshTokenAsync(ct); }
finally { _gate.Release(); }

Remember it is not re-entrant: if the same call chain takes it twice, it waits for itself forever.

No. The factory can run more than once for the same key; only one of the results is kept.

GetOrAdd runs your factory outside its internal lock. If 20 threads miss on key 42 at the same moment, up to 20 factories run, one value is stored, and all 20 callers get that same stored value. The dictionary stays correct, but an expensive load (a 300 ms query) runs many times.

To make the load run once per key, store a Lazy<T>. Creating the lazy is cheap, and its value is computed once:

var lazy = _map.GetOrAdd(id,
    k => new Lazy<Product>(() => Load(k)));
Product p = lazy.Value;

code.title: A deadlock from opposite lock order, and the fix

followUps:
In a deadlock the threads are asleep and wait forever; in a livelock they are awake and busy, but they keep reacting to each other and make no progress.

Picture two people in a corridor. Deadlock: both stand still, each waiting for the other to move. Livelock: both step left, then both step right, again and again.

In code: two threads each take one lock, fail to get the second with TryEnter, politely release, and retry at the same moment, forever. The difference shows on a dashboard: a deadlock has near 0% CPU, a livelock has high CPU and no finished work.

Fix a livelock by waiting a small random time before the retry, so the two stop moving in step.

Yes. The database has its own locks on rows and pages, and two transactions can block each other with no C# lock in sight.

Example: request 1 updates order 10 and then customer 7. Request 2 updates customer 7 and then order 10. Each holds one row lock and waits for the other.

The database detects the cycle and ends one transaction, the "victim". SQL Server reports error 1205. Your code should:

  • touch tables and rows in the same order everywhere;
  • keep transactions short, with no HTTP calls inside them;
  • have the right indexes, so fewer rows are locked;
  • retry the victim, for example with EF Core's EnableRetryOnFailure.

Take a dump of the process and look at what every thread is waiting for.

  1. Symptom: some requests never finish, CPU is low, and a restart "fixes" it.
  2. dotnet-stack report -p <pid> gives a quick list of all thread stacks. Look for threads stuck in Monitor.Enter or Task.Wait.
  3. dotnet-dump collect -p <pid>, then dotnet-dump analyze:
    • clrstack -all: the stack of every thread;
    • syncblk: which thread owns each lock, and how many wait for it.
  4. Thread 12 owns lock A and waits for B; thread 31 owns B and waits for A. That is the cycle.

For async code that never completes, dumpasync lists the paused state machines.

code.title: A bounded Channel with back-pressure, and an IAsyncEnumerable stream

followUps:
The writer is made to wait, or the item is dropped; which one depends on the FullMode you chose.

FullModeWhen the channel is full
Wait (default)WriteAsync waits without blocking a thread; TryWrite returns false
DropOldestThe oldest queued item is removed to make room
DropNewestThe newest queued item is removed
DropWriteThe item being written is thrown away

Example: capacity 500, a worker that handles 50 jobs per second and an API that receives 80. After about 17 seconds the channel is full. With Wait, the API can answer 429 when TryWrite fails. That is back-pressure, and it keeps memory flat.

Because BlockingCollection<T> waits by blocking a thread, and async code must never do that.

Take() on an empty collection parks the calling thread until an item arrives; Add() on a full one parks the producer. With 50 idle consumers you hold 50 threads that do nothing. Inside ASP.NET Core those are pool threads, so this pushes you toward thread-pool starvation.

Channel<T> offers the same queue with await reader.ReadAsync(ct) and await writer.WriteAsync(item, ct). A waiting reader costs a small object and no thread. BlockingCollection is still fine for a few dedicated threads in a console tool.

It streams the items: each one is written to the response as soon as it is produced, and the whole list is never held in memory.

app.MapGet("/orders", (ShopDb db) =>
    db.Orders.AsNoTracking().AsAsyncEnumerable());

The client receives one normal JSON array, [{...},{...}], that arrives piece by piece. For 1 million rows the server's memory stays flat, and the first bytes go out after the first row.

Points to mention:

  • The status code and headers are already sent, so an error half-way cuts the response short.
  • If the client disconnects, the request's token is cancelled and the query stops.
  • .NET 10 can also send such a stream as server-sent events with TypedResults.ServerSentEvents.

code.title: Task.WhenAll (no limit) vs Parallel.ForEachAsync (limit 5) vs PLINQ

followUps:
For computing work use the number of CPU cores; for waiting work use what the system on the other side can take, and find the number by measuring.

  • CPU-bound: more workers than cores only adds switching. Environment.ProcessorCount is the default.
  • I/O-bound: the limit is outside your process: the SQL connection pool (100 by default), an API rate limit, the other team's capacity.

Example: an API allows 100 requests per second and a call takes 200 ms. One worker makes 5 calls per second, so 20 workers reach the limit; I would start at 10.

Then load-test with 5, 10 and 20, and watch throughput and error rate. Stop raising when throughput stops growing or 429s and timeouts appear. Keep the number in configuration.

No. By default PLINQ returns results in whatever order the worker threads finish.

var a = Enumerable.Range(1, 8)
    .AsParallel().Select(n => n * 10).ToList();
// maybe 10, 50, 20, 60, 30, 70, 40, 80

var b = Enumerable.Range(1, 8)
    .AsParallel().AsOrdered().Select(n => n * 10).ToList();
// always 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80

AsOrdered() keeps the source order, at the price of extra buffering and some speed. If the order does not matter (a sum, a count, filling a set), leave it out. Also remember that PLINQ is for CPU work on data already in memory; it does not understand await.

It does not wait for the async work: Parallel.ForEach returns almost at once, while the real work is still running.

Parallel.ForEach expects a synchronous delegate. An async lambda there becomes async void. Each call "finishes", as far as the loop can see, at its first await. So:

  • the code after the loop runs before the items are processed;
  • there is no limit, all items are in flight at once;
  • an exception cannot be caught by the caller and can crash the process.

Fix (.NET 6 and later):

await Parallel.ForEachAsync(items,
    new ParallelOptions { MaxDegreeOfParallelism = 8 },
    async (x, ct) => await SendAsync(x, ct));

code.title: A thread-safe cache with expiry and one loader per key

followUps:
Absolute expiration removes the entry at a fixed time after it was stored; sliding expiration removes it only after nobody has read it for a set period, and every read restarts that period.

Absolute, 10 minSliding, 10 min
Stored at 12:00, read every minuteGone at 12:10Never expires
Stored at 12:00, never readGone at 12:10Gone at 12:10

The trap is the first row: with sliding only, a popular entry can serve data that is hours old. Use absolute for data that changes (prices, stock). Use sliding to drop rarely used entries, and combine it with an absolute cap:

new MemoryCacheEntryOptions {
    SlidingExpiration = TimeSpan.FromMinutes(10),
    AbsoluteExpirationRelativeToNow = TimeSpan.FromHours(1) };

An in-memory cache lives inside one process, so the other servers must be told: either through a shared cache, or with a message that says "this key changed".

  • Shared cache: keep the data in Redis. An update deletes the key once and every server sees it. Each read costs a network call of about 1 ms.
  • Two levels with a message: each server keeps a small local copy. On update, publish "product 42 changed" (Redis pub/sub or a Service Bus topic); every server removes its copy.
  • Short lifetime as a safety net: messages can be lost, so also give local entries a short expiry such as 30 to 60 seconds.

HybridCache (.NET 9 and later) gives the two levels in one API. State the staleness you accept: "up to 60 seconds old is fine for a product description, not for stock".

Because a failed task is also a value: if you cache it, every caller gets the same exception until the entry expires.

Example: at 12:00:00 the database has a 2-second blip and the load for product 42 fails. The cache now holds a faulted Task<Product> for 5 minutes. The database is healthy again at 12:00:02, yet the page keeps failing until 12:05.

A second trap: if the first caller's CancellationToken was passed to the load and that caller leaves, everyone waiting on the shared task gets a cancellation.

Fix: remove the entry when the task fails, and do not tie the shared load to one caller's token.

try { return await lazy.Value; }
catch { _map.TryRemove(key, out _); throw; }

code.title: Thread-pool starvation: 40 blocking waits vs 40 async waits

followUps:
Because threads are expensive, and for normal short work more threads than cores makes things slower, not faster.

  • Each thread reserves about 1 MB of stack (more on Linux by default), so 1,000 threads reserve a gigabyte or more.
  • With 8 cores and 1,000 runnable threads, the CPU spends its time switching between them.

So the pool starts with about one thread per core and then adds roughly one or two per second when work is waiting, while it measures whether more threads raise throughput. That is perfect for short tasks and far too slow for a burst of blocked ones: 300 blocked requests arriving in one second get only one or two new threads in that second, and the rest queue.

Starvation is extreme slowness that can recover; a deadlock is a full stop that never recovers.

StarvationDeadlock
ProgressSlow, a few requests finishNone for the threads involved
When load dropsThe queue drains and it healsStill stuck
Thread countKeeps climbingStable
In a dumpHundreds of threads blocked in Task.Wait, each on its own operationA cycle: thread 1 owns A and wants B, thread 2 owns B and wants A

Both show low CPU with stuck requests, which is why you need the dump or the counters to tell them apart.

The thread-pool queue length next to latency and CPU, because "slow while the CPU is idle" is the signature.

  • Thread-pool queue length. Healthy is near 0. Alert if it stays above 0 for a minute.
  • Thread-pool thread count. A steady climb, for example 30 to 300, means threads are being blocked.
  • 95th and 99th percentile response time on the same chart as CPU %.
  • Requests in progress and timeouts on outgoing calls, which often rise first.

These come from the built-in runtime metrics (in .NET 9 and later: dotnet.thread_pool.queue.length and dotnet.thread_pool.thread.count), visible live with dotnet-counters and exported through OpenTelemetry.

code.title: Value copy vs reference copy, and an object moving through GC generations

followUps:
No. A value type is on the stack only when it is a plain local variable; in many other cases it lives on the heap.

Where the value type isWhere it lives
Local variable int x = 5;Stack (or a CPU register)
Field of a class, e.g. order.TotalHeap, inside the object
Element of an array, new int[1000]Heap, inside the array
Boxed: object o = 5;Heap, in its own small object
Local captured by a lambda or used across an awaitHeap, as a field of a hidden class

The accurate sentence is: a value type is stored inline, wherever its container is. What defines it is copy-by-value, not the stack.

Because every large buffer you create with new lands on the Large Object Heap, and that heap is expensive to clean.

  • Arrays of 85,000 bytes or more skip gen 0 and go to the LOH.
  • The LOH is collected only during a full (gen 2) collection, the slowest kind.
  • It is not compacted by default, so holes form between blocks (fragmentation).

An endpoint that allocates a 1 MB buffer per request at 200 requests per second creates 200 MB of LOH garbage per second. Renting reuses the same few arrays:

byte[] buf = ArrayPool<byte>.Shared.Rent(1024 * 1024);
try { /* use buf[0..n] */ }
finally { ArrayPool<byte>.Shared.Return(buf); }

Rules: the rented array may be larger than asked and is not cleared, and you must not touch it after Return.

Workstation GC is tuned for one user and a small footprint; server GC is tuned for throughput on many cores and uses more memory to get it.

WorkstationServer
Heaps and GC threadsOne heapOne heap and one GC thread per core
Memory useLowerHigher
Throughput under loadLowerHigher
Typical useDesktop apps, small toolsASP.NET Core services

ASP.NET Core uses server GC by default when the machine has more than one core. A container limited to 1 CPU gets workstation GC. You choose with <ServerGarbageCollector> in the project file. Since .NET 9, server GC also adapts its number of heaps to the load, which lowers memory in small containers.

code.title: What keeps an object alive: an event subscription vs no reference

followUps:
The event stores a delegate, and the delegate holds a reference to the subscriber object, so the publisher points at the subscriber.

feed.PriceChanged += screen.OnPriceChanged creates a delegate with two parts: the method, and the Target, which is screen. The feed keeps that delegate in its list. The chain is: feed → delegate list → delegate → screen.

If the feed is a singleton or static, it is reachable for the whole run, so every screen that ever subscribed stays in memory, together with everything the screen references. Open the screen 1,000 times and you hold 1,000 screens.

Fix: unsubscribe with -= in Dispose. Note the direction: the subscriber is kept alive by the publisher, not the other way round.

gcroot in dotnet-dump prints the chain of references from a root down to one object.

  1. dotnet-dump collect -p <pid>, then dotnet-dump analyze <file>.
  2. dumpheap -stat: find the type with a suspicious count.
  3. dumpheap -type BasketViewModel: get the address of one instance.
  4. gcroot <address>:
static PriceFeed.Instance
 -> EventHandler (PriceChanged)
 -> BasketViewModel

The line just above your object is the reference to remove. Visual Studio's memory tool shows the same thing as "Paths to Root" when you open a dump or a dotnet-gcdump file, and PerfView can do it too.

When you want to use an object if it still exists, but you do not want to be the reason it stays in memory.

  • Weak events: a long-lived publisher keeps weak references to subscribers, so a forgotten unsubscribe does not leak a screen.
  • Extra data attached to an object you do not own: ConditionalWeakTable<TKey, TValue> drops the data when the key object dies.
  • A second chance for something rebuildable, such as a parsed template.
var weak = new WeakReference<Template>(template);
if (!weak.TryGetTarget(out Template t))
    t = Parse(path);      // it was collected: rebuild

It is a poor general cache: a weakly held object can vanish at the next gen 0 collection, milliseconds later. For caching use MemoryCache with a size limit and expiry.

code.title: The N+1 query problem: 51 round trips vs 2

followUps:
Count the SQL statements that one request sends: an N+1 shows up as the same query repeated many times with a different id.

  1. In a trace: open one slow request in Application Insights or any OpenTelemetry viewer. 1 request with 51 database calls of 2 ms each is the picture.
  2. In the logs: turn on EF Core command logging (Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Database.Command at Information) and look for SELECT ... WHERE Id = @p0 repeated.
  3. In code: a query or a lazy-loaded navigation property inside a foreach.

Fix: load it in one go with Include, or better a projection with Select that reads only the needed columns. Then add a test that fails if the endpoint sends more than, say, 3 queries.

A trustworthy number. BenchmarkDotNet handles the things that make a single Stopwatch reading wrong.

Problem with one Stopwatch runWhat BenchmarkDotNet does
The first call includes JIT compilationWarm-up runs that are not counted
One run is noiseMany runs; reports mean, error and standard deviation
A Debug build gives false resultsRefuses to run without optimizations
No view of memory[MemoryDiagnoser] shows bytes allocated and GC counts per call

Example: a stopwatch says 3 ms for a method; the benchmark says 180 ns and 96 bytes allocated. The 3 ms was almost all JIT. Stopwatch is still right for timing a whole request in production.

The 95th percentile (and often the 99th), because an average hides the users who are having a bad time.

Take 100 requests: 90 take 100 ms and 10 take 5,000 ms.

  • Average = (90 × 100 + 10 × 5,000) / 100 = 590 ms. It looks acceptable, and no user actually saw 590 ms.
  • 95th percentile = 5,000 ms. It says plainly that at least 1 user in 20 waits 5 seconds.

A percentile also stays calm when one request takes 60 seconds, where an average jumps. A good alert is tied to a target: "95th percentile of the checkout endpoint above 800 ms for 5 minutes", next to an error-rate alert.

code.title: Parsing with Split (allocates) vs ReadOnlySpan (no allocations)

followUps:
Because a span may point at memory on the stack, and an object on the heap can live longer than that stack memory.

Span<T> is a ref struct: a pointer plus a length. It can point into an array, into the middle of a string, or at a stackalloc buffer that disappears when the method returns. If a class could store it, the object could outlive the buffer and read freed memory.

So the compiler keeps spans on the stack only: no class fields, no boxing, no arrays of spans, no capture in a lambda, and not across an await.

When you need to store a buffer or carry it across an await, use Memory<T> and call .Span where you do the work:

class Parser { private Memory<byte> _buffer; }

When the size is large or comes from outside, because the stack is small and overflowing it kills the process.

A thread's stack is about 1 MB by default (8 MB on many Linux setups). stackalloc byte[n] with n from user input, or a modest stackalloc inside a loop or deep recursion, can use it up. The result is a StackOverflowException, which no try/catch can handle: the whole service goes down.

Safe habit: a small fixed limit, and the pool for anything bigger.

byte[] rented = null;
Span<byte> buf = len <= 256
    ? stackalloc byte[256]
    : (rented = ArrayPool<byte>.Shared.Rent(len));
try { /* use buf.Slice(0, len) */ }
finally { if (rented != null) ArrayPool<byte>.Shared.Return(rented); }

Span<T> lets you read and write the memory it points at; ReadOnlySpan<T> lets you only read.

int[] data = { 1, 2, 3 };
Span<int> s = data;
s[0] = 10;                       // fine: data[0] is now 10
ReadOnlySpan<int> r = data;
// r[0] = 10;                    // compile error
ReadOnlySpan<char> text = "hello".AsSpan();   // strings give only read-only spans
  • A string is immutable, so slicing it gives ReadOnlySpan<char>.
  • A Span<T> converts to ReadOnlySpan<T> automatically, not the other way.
  • For a method that only reads, take ReadOnlySpan<T>: it accepts arrays, strings, slices and stack buffers, and promises the caller its data will not change.

code.title: A managed leak: an unbounded static list vs a bounded one

followUps:
I check, in this order, the five things that are quick to answer and that cover most real cases.

  1. Managed or native? Compare the GC heap size with the process memory. If the heap is flat while the process grows, the leak is in native memory, and a heap dump will not show it.
  2. Static and singleton collections that only ever get Add.
  3. Caches with no size limit or no expiry, including a Dictionary used as a cache.
  4. Events, timers and CancellationTokenSource registrations that are never removed or disposed.
  5. What changed in the release where the memory graph started to slope.

If none of these gives the answer in 15 minutes, I stop guessing and take two dotnet-gcdump snapshots a few hours apart.

A warming cache flattens out; a leak keeps climbing for as long as there is traffic.

Look at the memory that remains after full collections over a long period:

HourCache warming upLeak
1300 MB300 MB
6650 MB700 MB
24700 MB1,900 MB
48700 MBout of memory

Three checks: does the curve level off; does the cache have a known maximum (10,000 entries of 50 KB is 500 MB, so 700 MB is plausible); and in two heap snapshots, is the growing type the cache entry, with a count at or below the limit? A cache with no limit is a leak with a nicer name.

Because every new HttpClient opens its own connections, so nothing is reused and the machine runs out of network ports.

  • Each request pays for a new TCP connection and a new TLS handshake, often 50 to 100 ms extra.
  • When the client is disposed, the closed sockets stay reserved by the operating system for a while. At a few hundred requests per second you get SocketException errors about addresses already in use.
  • If the clients are not disposed either, their handlers and connections pile up, and it looks like a memory and handle leak.

Fix: builder.Services.AddHttpClient<PaymentClient>() and inject the client. The factory shares a small pool of handlers and renews them every few minutes, so connections are reused and DNS changes are still picked up.

code.title: Daily modern C#: nullable types, records, patterns, init/required

followUps:
Nothing. Nullable reference types are a compile-time check only; the compiled program behaves exactly the same.

The compiler tracks whether each reference may be null and gives warnings, for example when you write customer.Email.Length while Email is string?. The ? is metadata for the compiler, not a new type, so a null can still reach a string at run time (from JSON, reflection or old code) and cause a NullReferenceException.

Practical advice: turn it on with <Nullable>enable</Nullable>, treat warnings as errors in new projects, and validate data at the edges of the system.

Don't use a record for things that have an identity and change over time, such as an entity with an id, or for a class that holds behaviour more than data.

  • An EF Core entity: two Order rows with equal data are still different orders, and tracking needs reference identity.
  • A service class with dependencies and mutable state.
  • A very hot data type that is copied a lot: a record is a class, so consider a record struct.

Records fit DTOs, API requests and responses, messages, and value objects such as Money. Rule of thumb: if two instances with equal data should be interchangeable, use a record.

with makes a copy of a record and lets you change some properties in the copy; the original stays untouched.

var a = new Money(10m, "EUR");
var b = a with { Amount = 25m };
// a: Money { Amount = 10, Currency = EUR }
// b: Money { Amount = 25, Currency = EUR }

It is how you "change" immutable data: you build a new value. This is shallow: a list inside the record is shared between both copies, not duplicated. Cost is one allocation for a record class and none for a record struct.

code.title: Features by C# version, in one program

followUps:
Yes, to a large extent, because most new features are compiler-only; but some need runtime support, so you cannot always.

Set <LangVersion>latest</LangVersion> and the compiler accepts new syntax while still targeting an older .NET. Records and init work on .NET Framework 4.8 if you add a small polyfill class (IsExternalInit). Features that need new runtime types or behaviour do not work: default interface members and ref-field spans need a runtime that has them.

Also, Microsoft supports each C# version only with its matching SDK and default framework. For production I would upgrade the target framework, not fight with polyfills.

Records came with C# 9 (.NET 5), and record structs with C# 10 (.NET 6).

  • record (C# 9): a class with value equality, with and a nice ToString.
  • record struct (C# 10): the same ideas on a struct. readonly record struct is immutable and avoids heap allocation.

Memory aid: C# 9 = records, init, top-level statements; C# 10 = file-scoped namespaces, global usings, record structs. Pick the struct form for small, hot values (a point, an amount), the class form for bigger data.

LTS means long-term support: 3 years of fixes. STS (standard-term support) used to be 18 months and is now 24 months.

LTSSTS
VersionsEven numbers: .NET 6, 8, 10Odd numbers: .NET 7, 9
Support3 years2 years
Use forProduction services that you upgrade rarelyTeams that upgrade every year

Check the official support policy page for the current end dates before you promise a deadline to a team. As of late 2026, .NET 10 is the LTS to be on.

code.title: What C# 14 features expand to (written out in C# 12 so it runs anywhere)

followUps:
An extension method looks like an instance method; an extension property (new in C# 14) looks like a property, so you can write text.IsBlank and not text.IsBlank().

They are declared together in an extension(string text) { ... } block. Besides properties, the block can hold methods and, inside it, static members and operators on the type, which old extension methods could not do.

Use a property when it is cheap, has no arguments and reads like a fact about the object (IsBlank, Count). Keep a method for anything that does work or can fail. Existing this-style extension methods keep working.

It removes the need for a hand-written private field when you only want a little logic in a property setter or getter.

Before C# 14, adding trimming to one setter meant writing it all out:

private string _name = "";
public string Name { get => _name; set => _name = value.Trim(); }

Now: public string Name { get; set => field = value.Trim(); }. The compiler generates the backing field, and field is only usable inside that accessor. One warning: if you already have a member called field, write @field or this.field to refer to it.

Treat it as a small, repeated project: one template, one pilot, then the rest in waves, with tests and metrics guarding each step.

  1. Inventory: list each service, its packages and the Dockerfile base image.
  2. Prepare in one place: central package management and one global.json; read the breaking-change notes for the releases in between.
  3. Pilot 2 services: change TargetFramework to net10.0, update packages, fix warnings, run the tests, load test.
  4. Waves of 3 to 5 services, lowest risk first, each with a canary deployment and a rollback.
  5. Track done and remaining on a board. Dependabot or Renovate keeps packages current afterwards.

Reason to hurry: .NET 8 support ends in November 2026.

code.title: SOLID in small steps: SRP, OCP and DIP with plain C#

followUps:
Single Responsibility, in the form of the "manager" class: one class that validates, saves, sends email and writes the log.

You see it as a file of 800 lines, 9 constructor parameters, and tests that need 9 mocks. Every change in any of the four jobs touches the same class, so merge conflicts and regressions are frequent.

Fix by splitting along reasons to change: a validator, a repository, a notifier, and a small service that coordinates them. Do not start with a framework of 20 classes; split when a second reason to change actually shows up.

Because a square forced to inherit from a rectangle breaks what callers expect of a rectangle.

void Resize(Rectangle r)
{
    r.Width = 5; r.Height = 10;
    // caller expects area 50
}

If a Square is passed, setting the width also sets the height, so the area is 100 and the caller is surprised. Liskov says a subtype must work wherever its base type is used without surprising the caller.

In real code the same error looks like a subclass that throws NotSupportedException for an inherited method (a read-only collection derived from a list). Fix: do not inherit; use a common read-only interface or make the shapes immutable.

Yes: applying SOLID to code that has no second implementation and no reason to change creates layers that only add reading time.

Example: an IOrderIdGenerator interface, an OrderIdGenerator, a factory for it, and a registration for each, to produce Guid.NewGuid(). Five files and one implementation that will never be swapped.

A good test: can you name the second implementation or the test that needs a fake? If not, write the concrete class. Extract the interface the day the second need shows up; with a modern IDE this is a 30-second refactoring.

code.title: A tiny DI container with lifetimes: transient, scoped, singleton

followUps:
That is a "captive dependency": the singleton lives for the whole app and keeps the scoped object alive far too long, so one request's data (for example a DbContext) is shared by all later requests.

Effects: stale cached entities, thread-safety bugs because a DbContext is not thread-safe, and connections never released. In development ASP.NET Core checks this (ValidateScopes) and throws "Cannot consume scoped service from singleton".

Fix: make the consumer scoped, or inject IServiceScopeFactory and create a scope per operation:

using var scope = _scopes.CreateScope();
var db = scope.ServiceProvider.GetRequiredService<ShopDb>();

This is also how a BackgroundService must use scoped services.

Constructor injection, because it makes the dependencies visible and the object complete from the first moment.

  • You cannot create the object without its dependencies, so there is no half-built state.
  • Fields can be readonly.
  • A constructor with 8 parameters is a visible warning that the class does too much.

Property injection hides what is needed, allows null at run time, and the built-in ASP.NET Core container does not support it. The exceptions are optional dependencies, and framework-created classes where you cannot change the constructor. With C# 12 a primary constructor makes this short: class OrderService(IRepo repo).

Yes. DI is a way of passing dependencies in; a container is only a tool that does the wiring for you.

Doing it by hand is called "pure DI" and the wiring happens in one place, the composition root:

var repo = new SqlRepo(connectionString);
var mail = new SmtpMailer(host);
var service = new OrderService(repo, mail);

It is perfectly fine for a small console tool or for tests. A container adds lifetimes (scoped per request), automatic wiring of big graphs, and disposal of what it created. Use one when the graph gets large, not before.

code.title: DRY gone wrong, "tell, don't ask", and the Law of Demeter

followUps:
A common one: two screens both show "price with tax", so someone merges them into one function with a flag for each difference, and the function grows into a mess.

Example: Format(order, isInvoice, isEmail, showTax, shortForm). The invoice and the email only looked alike. When the tax law changes the invoice, the email also changes and breaks, and each caller needs to know which flag combination is safe.

Rule of thumb: duplicate code is cheaper than the wrong abstraction. Merge only when both copies change for the same reason. If a shared function needs a boolean parameter to switch between uses, split it again.

It keeps tests small, because an object that talks only to its direct neighbours needs only those neighbours faked.

Code like order.Customer.Address.City forces a test to build an order, a customer and an address just to check one city. If the method takes a string city or the order exposes order.ShippingCity, the test needs one value.

Chains also tie callers to the inner structure: if Address moves, every caller breaks. Note that fluent APIs such as query.Where(...).Select(...) are fine; they return the same kind of object, they do not dig through different objects.

The rule of three says: copy once if you must, and extract a shared abstraction only when the same code appears a third time.

Two copies are too little information to know what truly stays the same. By the third you can see which parts vary and which are fixed, so the shared function gets the right shape. Extracting at two often produces an abstraction that the third case does not fit, and that is harder to fix than a duplicate.

It is a guide, not a law: if the duplicated code is a security check or a business rule that must never differ, extract it at two.

code.title: Replacing a type switch with polymorphism, and a testable clock

followUps:
Start with the code, not the person, and agree on a shared goal such as "the next change should be easy".

  1. Ask a question instead of giving an order: "If we add a fourth discount type next month, which files will we edit?"
  2. Show a small concrete cost: "Every new type touches 6 files; here are the last 3 pull requests."
  3. Offer a minimal change and say you accept their view if they show a reason for the simple version.
  4. Check with data: bug count in that file, time per change.

If you still disagree, the tech lead decides, and writes the reason in the pull request or a short ADR. Experience means the senior is often right about context you lack; stay open to that.

A switch is fine when the set of cases is small, fixed and local: one place decides, and no other file repeats the same switch.

  • Mapping an enum that is part of a protocol (HTTP method, day of week) to a result.
  • A switch expression that is the only place that knows the cases, with a compiler warning for missing ones.
  • The edge of a system: parsing a message type into the right handler.

It becomes a smell when the same switch (type) shows up in three files, so each new case means three edits. Then move the behaviour into the types, or use a lookup table of handlers.

Don't call it in the code you want to test; get the time from an object you can replace. Since .NET 8 the built-in type is TimeProvider.

class Subscription(TimeProvider clock, DateTime end)
{
    public bool IsActive() => clock.GetUtcNow() < end;
}
// test: new FakeTimeProvider(start) from
// Microsoft.Extensions.TimeProvider.Testing
// fake.Advance(TimeSpan.FromDays(31));

In production you register TimeProvider.System. The test moves time forward instantly, so a "30-day trial expires" test takes milliseconds and never fails because of the real date. Also use UTC for stored times.

code.title: Attributes read by reflection: mask sensitive properties

followUps:
Typical answers, each with what reads it:

AttributeRead by
[ApiController], [HttpGet], [Route]ASP.NET Core routing and model binding
[Required], [MaxLength(50)]Model validation and EF Core model building
[Authorize]The authorization middleware
[JsonPropertyName("id")]System.Text.Json
[Fact]The xUnit test runner

The point to show: an attribute does nothing alone; some framework code must look for it.

Look up the member once and keep it, or better, avoid reflection at run time: compiled expressions, delegates or a source generator.

  1. Cache the PropertyInfo, MethodInfo or Type in a static field; finding it is the expensive part.
  2. Turn it into a delegate: Delegate.CreateDelegate or a compiled expression tree, which then calls at nearly normal speed.
  3. Source generators (System.Text.Json, regex, logging) write the plain C# at build time, so nothing is reflected at run time and Native AOT works.

Example: 1,000,000 calls through a cached PropertyInfo.GetValue take around 20 to 50 ms, a compiled delegate about 2 ms. Measure with BenchmarkDotNet before bothering.

Yes, with BindingFlags.NonPublic, and almost always you should not.

It breaks the class's promise: private fields are private so the author can change them. After a rename in the next release, your code fails at run time, not at compile time, and nobody sees it in a search for usages. It also bypasses validation in setters.

Acceptable uses are narrow: serializers and test or diagnostic tools, and old third-party code you cannot change. Prefer a public API, InternalsVisibleTo for tests, or [UnsafeAccessor] (.NET 8 and later), which gives fast, typed access to a private member without reflection.

code.title: System.Text.Json: options, enums, casing and polymorphism

followUps:
Because each new instance builds its own cache of type information, and that is slow and allocates a lot.

The first time the serializer sees a type it uses reflection to learn its properties and builds converters, stored per options object. A new JsonSerializerOptions on each call throws the cache away, so you pay that cost every request. It also makes memory grow, because the old caches are kept for a while.

static readonly JsonSerializerOptions Options = new(JsonSerializerDefaults.Web);
// ... JsonSerializer.Serialize(x, Options);

Once you use an options object, it becomes read-only. ASP.NET Core already has one shared instance configured through ConfigureHttpJsonOptions.

Use polymorphism attributes on the base class: [JsonPolymorphic] and one [JsonDerivedType] per child (.NET 7 and later).

[JsonDerivedType(typeof(Circle), "circle")]
[JsonDerivedType(typeof(Square), "square")]
[JsonDerivedType(typeof(Triangle), "triangle")]
abstract class Shape { }

The JSON gets a "$type": "circle" discriminator on writing and is read back into the right class. Only types you list are allowed, which also protects against a client asking you to create an arbitrary type. Before .NET 7 you had to write a custom JsonConverter.

Several defaults differ, and the differences cause silent bugs, so test the real payloads.

  • Casing: Newtonsoft matches names without regard to case; System.Text.Json is case-sensitive unless you use the Web defaults or PropertyNameCaseInsensitive.
  • Numbers in strings such as "5" are rejected unless you enable NumberHandling.
  • Fields and private setters: only public properties by default; fields need IncludeFields.
  • Missing features: no JObject (use JsonNode), different handling of circular references, and no support for some attributes.
  • Enums are numbers unless you add JsonStringEnumConverter.

Plan: switch one API at a time, with contract tests on its JSON.

code.title: What a source generator emits: partial class, compile-time code

followUps:
Turn on the compiler output in the project file, and the generated files are written to disk where you can open them.

<PropertyGroup>
  <EmitCompilerGeneratedFiles>true</EmitCompilerGeneratedFiles>
  <CompilerGeneratedFilesOutputPath>obj/generated</CompilerGeneratedFilesOutputPath>
</PropertyGroup>

In Visual Studio, expand Dependencies → Analyzers → the generator in Solution Explorer; in Rider, the same under the project's generated files. You can also press F12 on a generated member and the IDE opens the generated source. Reading this output is the quickest way to debug a generator or to see what [LoggerMessage] or [GeneratedRegex] really produce.

An incremental generator is one that remembers its earlier work, so the IDE does not redo everything on each keystroke.

The older ISourceGenerator ran from the start on every change, which made editing slow in large solutions. IIncrementalGenerator describes a pipeline: pick the interesting syntax nodes, turn them into small value objects, and generate code from those. If the value object did not change after an edit, the cached output is reused.

Rule for authors: keep the pipeline steps cheap and compare simple data (records, strings), never keep Roslyn symbols in the cache. New generators should always be incremental.

The rules that you would otherwise repeat in every code review, because a rule enforced by the compiler never needs a reviewer to remember it.

  • No .Result, .Wait() or async void in the web projects.
  • No DateTime.Now; use TimeProvider.
  • Project-specific: "controllers must not use DbContext directly", "every public API method needs a CancellationToken".
  • Naming and style, through .editorconfig severity settings.

Start with warnings, fix the old ones, then raise the rule to an error so the build fails. Ready-made packages (Roslynator, the Microsoft threading analyzers) cover many of these before you write your own.

code.title: Why reflection is hard to trim: names looked up as text

followUps:
Choose it when start-up time, memory or file size matter more than the full flexibility of the runtime: serverless functions, containers that scale to zero, command-line tools, and sidecars.

  • A function that starts in 20 to 50 ms and not 300 to 600 ms is the difference between a cold start the user notices or not.
  • No JIT and no runtime to ship, so the image is small and memory use is lower.

Don't choose it for a large app that depends on reflection-heavy libraries (some ORMs, dynamic proxies, plugins loaded at run time) or when you need peak throughput over hours: the JIT can optimize the hot code further. Check first that every package is AOT-compatible.

ReadyToRun (R2R) pre-compiles code to native code but keeps the runtime and the JIT, while Native AOT removes them.

ReadyToRunNative AOT
Needs the .NET runtime on the machineYesNo, one self-contained native file
Reflection, dynamic loadingFully supportedRestricted
Start-upFaster than plain JITFastest
Peak speedSame, the JIT can recompile hot codeSlightly lower

R2R is the low-risk step: add <PublishReadyToRun>true</PublishReadyToRun> and nothing in your code has to change.

Look for the trim-safety information in the package, then test it with the analyzers and a real publish.

  1. The package's description or repository says whether it supports trimming or AOT (look for IsTrimmable / IsAotCompatible in its project file).
  2. In your project set <IsAotCompatible>true</IsAotCompatible>. The build then reports warnings such as IL2026 and IL3050 where a call is not safe.
  3. Run dotnet publish -r linux-x64 -p:PublishAot=true and watch for warnings that come from inside the package.
  4. Run the published binary and your integration tests. A warning-free publish can still fail at run time.

If a package is not safe, look for a source-generated alternative or isolate it in a service that does not use AOT.

code.title: API design: invalid states impossible, read-only results, safe growth

followUps:
Because it tells callers what they may do and hides what they must not, so you can change the inside later.

  • List<T> lets the caller add, remove and clear. If you return your own internal list, they can break your state.
  • A List<T> in the signature is a promise to always keep a list; you could never switch to an array or a lazy sequence without a breaking change.
  • IReadOnlyList<T> still gives count and indexing, which is what most callers need.

Remember that a read-only interface over your own list is a view, and the owner can still change it. Where callers must hold a stable snapshot, return a copy or an ImmutableArray<T>. For parameters, accept the widest type you need, such as IEnumerable<T>.

Yes, for binary compatibility, and sometimes for source compatibility too.

Default values are copied by the compiler into the caller's code. A method Send(string to) changed to Send(string to, bool urgent = false) is a different method in the compiled file. Callers that were compiled earlier still look for Send(string), which no longer exists: a MissingMethodException at run time until they rebuild.

Also changing the default value later does not reach callers who have not recompiled.

Safe way: keep the old method and add a new overload, then mark the old one [Obsolete] in a later version.

Document with XML comments and samples, and test the public surface the way a caller would use it, not just the internals.

  • Docs: /// summary, parameters, exceptions, and one usage example for each main type. Turn on GenerateDocumentationFile and treat a missing comment on a public member as a warning.
  • Tests: unit tests through the public API only; a sample project that uses the package from NuGet; a test that fails if the public API changes by accident, using a published API snapshot or the PublicApiAnalyzers package (which keeps PublicAPI.Shipped.txt).
  • Versioning: semantic versioning and a changelog.

code.title: Result pattern: expected failures as return values, mapped to HTTP codes

followUps:
It can spread boilerplate: every call must check the result, and a forgotten check silently ignores an error.

  • Code gets longer: if (!r.IsSuccess) return r; after each call, where an exception would travel up by itself.
  • Callers can read .Value of a failed result and get null or a default.
  • Mixing styles: some methods return results, others throw, and nobody knows which.
  • Real failures (a bug, a network error) still arrive as exceptions, so you need both.

Rule: use results for failures the caller can plan for (validation, not found, conflicts) at the service boundary, and keep exceptions for the unexpected. Don't wrap every small method in a result.

At the edge of the application, in the controller or minimal API endpoint, in one shared place, not inside the business code.

The service knows "not found" and "conflict"; it should not know about HTTP. The endpoint maps once:

return result.Error switch
{
    null => Results.Ok(result.Value),
    Errors.NotFound => Results.Problem(statusCode: 404),
    Errors.Conflict => Results.Problem(statusCode: 409),
    _ => Results.Problem(statusCode: 400)
};

With a shared extension method, every endpoint uses the same table, so the API answers consistently. The same service can then be used from a background job or a console tool without any HTTP types.

Because a stack trace shows the inside of your system to an attacker and means nothing to a client.

  • It exposes class names, file paths, library versions and sometimes SQL or connection details, which helps someone plan an attack.
  • The client cannot act on it, but your support team can: log the full exception with a correlation id.

Return a Problem Details body (RFC 9457) with a stable type, a title, the status and a traceId. In ASP.NET Core call AddProblemDetails() and UseExceptionHandler(), and show detail only in the Development environment. Support then asks the user for the trace id and finds the full error in the logs.

code.title: Review checklist as tests: three bugs a reviewer should spot

followUps:
Don't read it line by line. Ask the author to split it, and if that is impossible, review in layers.

  1. Start with the description and the tests: do they match the goal? A 2,000-line PR without tests is a finding by itself.
  2. Look at the shape first: new files, deleted files, changed public APIs, database migrations. Ask "which 200 lines carry the risk?"
  3. Read those risky parts closely (security, money, data changes).
  4. Skim generated code, renames and moves, and rely on the build and tools.

Then give the author a clear request: "Please split into a refactor PR and a behaviour PR". A pair review on a call of 30 minutes can also be faster than 10 comment rounds. For the future, agree on a size target such as under 400 lines.

Review it exactly like human code, with extra care on the things AI gets wrong, and ask the author to explain it.

  • The author owns every line: "I can explain this" is the rule. If they cannot, it does not merge.
  • Check for invented APIs and package names that do not exist, a confident-looking but wrong edge case, and missing cancellation tokens.
  • Look for hidden problems: .Result, a new HttpClient per call, secrets in code, over-engineering with extra layers.
  • Read the tests: AI tests often assert what the code does, not what it should do.

Run the code and the tests; do not trust that it looks right.

Move from opinions to facts, then to a decision: write down both options, the trade-offs, and who decides.

  1. Ask each to state the concrete risk or benefit in a sentence ("this lock will block under load" is checkable; "I prefer it" is not).
  2. If it can be tested, test it: a quick benchmark or a failing test settles many arguments.
  3. Check the team's guidelines or an earlier ADR.
  4. If it stays a style matter, apply the existing rule or let the author choose, and move on.
  5. If it matters, the tech lead decides in the thread, and records the reason.

Take it out of the pull request comments into a 10-minute call when it has gone back and forth more than twice.

code.title: Breaking change in steps: add new, mark old obsolete, keep it working

followUps:
Because the default value is baked into the calling code at compile time, and the compiled signature is different.

Version 1: Send(string to). Version 2: Send(string to, bool urgent = false). At the call site Send("a") the compiler writes a call to Send(string, bool) with false copied in. A team that did not recompile still calls Send(string) (version 1), which no longer exists in the new DLL, so it throws MissingMethodException.

It also means changing the default later has no effect until callers recompile. Avoid it in a shared library: add an overload and keep the old method.

They let you add a new method to an interface without breaking classes that already implement it, because the interface supplies a default body.

public interface IPriceSource
{
    decimal Get(int id);
    decimal Get(int id, string currency) => Get(id); // new, default body
}

Old implementers still compile and run. Limits: the default is reachable only through the interface type, not on the class variable; it can hide a design that should be a new interface; and once released you cannot remove the member without a break. Use them for evolving an interface, not as a general replacement for abstract classes.

At least one major version and long enough for every team to move, in practice 6 to 12 months, and announced with a date.

  1. Mark it [Obsolete] with a message that says what to use instead and in which version it will go.
  2. Keep it as a warning for a full release cycle, then raise it to an error ([Obsolete("...", error: true)]) in the next minor version.
  3. Remove it only in the next major version.

Check real usage before removing: search the company's code or telemetry to see who still calls it, and talk to those teams. A deprecation policy written down in the library's README ("we remove after two minor releases and 6 months") stops arguments.

code.title: DDD tactical patterns: value object, entity and aggregate rule

followUps:
Draw the line around the data that must be consistent together in one transaction; everything else is a separate aggregate that you reference by id.

  • Ask: "what rule needs these objects to be correct at the same moment?" An order and its lines must (the total must match the lines), so they are one aggregate.
  • A customer's name and their orders do not need to change together, so Customer and Order are two aggregates, and the order holds only a CustomerId.
  • Keep aggregates small. A big one means locking and concurrency conflicts, and slow loading.

Rule of thumb: one transaction changes one aggregate. Changes across aggregates are done with events and are eventually consistent.

With OwnsOne (or ComplexProperty in EF Core 8 and later), so the value object's fields become columns in the owner's table.

modelBuilder.Entity<Order>()
    .ComplexProperty(o => o.Total, m =>
    {
        m.Property(x => x.Amount).HasColumnName("TotalAmount");
        m.Property(x => x.Currency).HasColumnName("TotalCurrency").HasMaxLength(3);
    });

The value object has no key and no table of its own. For a single-value type like EmailAddress, a value converter (HasConversion) stores it as one string column. Collections of value objects use OwnsMany and get their own table with a hidden key.

An anaemic domain model is a set of classes that hold only data (properties with getters and setters), while all the rules live in separate "service" classes.

The problem: nothing stops any code from putting an object into an invalid state, such as setting order.Status = Shipped on an empty order. The same rule gets copied into several services, or forgotten.

The cure is behaviour on the object: order.Place() checks the rules and is the only way to change the status; setters become private.

Don't over-correct: for a simple CRUD screen without rules, plain data classes are fine, and DDD is not worth its cost there.

Because strings can be shared between unrelated parts of the program, so your lock may be taken by someone else's code and cause a deadlock.

.NET stores identical string literals only once (string interning). If class A does lock ("config") and a completely different class B in another library also does lock ("config"), both lock the same object, even though they have nothing to do with each other. They wait for one another, and the bug is almost impossible to find by reading code.

The same problem applies to lock (this) and lock (typeof(X)), which outsiders can also lock. Always lock a private object: private readonly object _gate = new(); or, from .NET 9, new Lock().

Lazy<T> has three thread-safety modes, chosen with LazyThreadSafetyMode.

ModeWhat happens
ExecutionAndPublication (default)A lock makes sure the factory runs once; other threads wait for the value
PublicationOnlySeveral threads may run the factory; the first finished value wins, the others are thrown away
NoneNo thread safety; fastest, for single-threaded use

Use the default when the factory is expensive or has side effects. A detail worth knowing: in the default mode an exception from the factory is cached and thrown on every access.

Both are compiled into a state machine that pauses at a keyword and continues from the same place when asked again.

With yield return, the method pauses and hands one item to the caller; it resumes when the caller asks for the next item (MoveNext). With await, the method pauses until a task finishes; it resumes when that task completes. Local variables are kept as fields of a hidden class in both cases, and a "state" number says where to continue.

An async iterator (async IAsyncEnumerable<T>) combines both: it can await while it produces items.

Rarely; it is acceptable in a few narrow cases where you know a moment when a big collection will help.

  • Benchmarks and tests that measure memory, so earlier runs do not distort the numbers.
  • After a rare, huge, one-time job, for example loading a 2 GB file at start-up and releasing it, in a long-running desktop tool.
  • Right before you take a memory snapshot, to see only real survivors.

In a web service, don't: the GC knows better when to run, and forcing a full collection pauses threads and throws away its tuning. If you feel the need, the real cause is usually a leak or too many allocations. If memory is high at idle, adjust the GC settings, not the code.

Pick the method that fits the type, because there is no built-in "deep clone" in .NET.

  • Records and immutable data: a shallow copy with with is enough, as nothing changes.
  • Serialize and read back (System.Text.Json): simple and works for plain data. It loses private state and is slow.
  • A copy constructor or Clone() method written by hand: explicit and fast, but you must update it when fields are added.
  • A source generator that writes the copy code at build time.

Don't use BinaryFormatter: it is removed for security reasons. Watch for shared references (two fields pointing to the same list) and cycles.

Yes, a struct can implement an interface, but using it through the interface boxes it, which means copying it to the heap.

struct Point : IComparable<Point> { public int X; /* ... */ }

Point p = new Point();
IComparable<Point> c = p;   // boxing: allocation + copy
c.CompareTo(...)              // works on the boxed copy

Consequences: an allocation each time, and a mutation through the interface changes only the boxed copy, not your variable. To avoid boxing, use a generic constraint: void Sort<T>(T a) where T : struct, IComparable<T>. The JIT then makes a specialized version for the struct, with a direct call and no allocation. That is how generic collections of structs stay fast.
